tagline: A friendly weekly read on what actually moved in AI.
editor_note: Issue five, and it was a week about who's in charge. Apple handed Siri's brain to Google and cracked the door open to Claude and ChatGPT. OpenAI quietly filed to go public at a price tag with twelve zeros. And Washington drew a hard line around Anthropic's best models — so hard it locked out one of the field's most famous researchers. Plus a study that asks whether your chatbot and a bumblebee have anything in common. 🐝

stories.title: Apple gives Siri a Gemini brain — and a model picker
stories.why_you_care: The assistant on a billion iPhones is being rebuilt on someone else's AI — and for the first time you'll get to choose whose.
stories.body: At WWDC on June 8, Apple unveiled a completely rebuilt Siri running on a custom 1.2-trillion-parameter version of Google's Gemini, hosted in Google Cloud under a deal reportedly worth roughly $1 billion a year. The bigger shift for users is the new Extensions framework arriving in iOS 27: a setting that lets you swap the model behind Siri between Google's Gemini, OpenAI's ChatGPT, and Anthropic's Claude (the first time Claude has been a built-in iPhone option). Notably, Apple described the Extensions system but declined to demo it live.
stories.more: Read this as Apple admitting it lost the race to build a frontier model and choosing to become the place you pick one instead. That's a real strategy — owning the device and the defaults can matter more than owning the model — but it also makes Apple a landlord renting from its biggest rival. Watch two things: whether the Extensions picker actually ships on time (the no-demo is a yellow flag), and whether 'choose your AI' becomes the norm other platforms copy.

stories.title: OpenAI files for a ~$1 trillion IPO
stories.why_you_care: The company that started the chatbot era is heading for the stock market, and its books are about to become public — a real test of whether the AI boom pencils out.
stories.body: OpenAI confidentially filed its IPO paperwork with the SEC, confirmed publicly on June 8, with Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and JPMorgan leading a deal that targets a valuation as high as $1 trillion (a confidential filing lets regulators review the financials before they're shown to the public). A debut could come as early as September. The filing reportedly shows around $2 billion in monthly revenue — but the company doesn't expect to be profitable until 2030.
stories.more: If it prices near $1T, this would be the largest IPO in history. The tension the prospectus exposes is the whole AI trade in miniature: enormous, fast-growing revenue against enormous losses, with profitability years out. OpenAI itself hinted it's in no rush — some things are 'easier as a private company.' Anthropic filed its own confidential prospectus a week earlier at $965B, so 2026 may be remembered as the year frontier AI grew up and went public.

stories.title: Washington walls off Anthropic's top models
stories.why_you_care: The US just treated frontier AI like a weapon system — which decides who, anywhere on earth, is allowed to use the most capable models.
stories.body: On June 14, reports said the US government issued an export-control directive ordering Anthropic to suspend access to its most advanced models — Fable 5 and Mythos 5 — for any foreign national, whether inside or outside the country, including Anthropic's own non-citizen employees. The most striking casualty: Andrej Karpathy, the renowned OpenAI co-founder who joined Anthropic's pre-training team in May, is now reportedly barred from the company's top model because he isn't a US citizen.
stories.more: Export controls have long governed chips; extending them to the models themselves is a meaningful escalation. The immediate friction is practical — global labs run on global talent, and rules drawn around citizenship cut straight through their own teams. The longer game is geopolitical: if frontier models are national-security assets, access becomes a lever of statecraft, and 'who can use the best AI' starts to look like 'who can buy the best fighter jet.' Watch whether other labs face the same order.

quick_hits.text: That's the revenue OpenAI's IPO paperwork reportedly shows — roughly $24B a year — yet the company says it won't turn a profit until 2030, a reminder that scale and profitability are still very different things in AI.

Anthropic's first-generation Claude 4 API models stop accepting requests on June 15, with Claude Sonnet 4.8 expected to land within days — the steady Opus-then-Sonnet cadence holding after Opus 4.8 shipped in late May.

A Tufts neuro-symbolic robot system — neural nets paired with human-style step-by-step reasoning — hit a 95% success rate on a planning task versus 34% for standard models while drawing a fraction of the energy, the efficiency-over-scale thesis now showing up in robotics.

Europe's Mistral roughly doubled its valuation in a Series C led by chip-equipment giant ASML, with Nvidia joining — the continent's flagship lab scaling fast, even at about 1/60th of Anthropic's worth.

quick_hits.lede: Apple built the picker but wouldn't show it.
quick_hits.text: The 'choose your AI' Extensions system for Siri was announced but never demoed live at WWDC — a quiet signal that the most interesting part of Apple's AI pitch may not be as ready as the keynote implied.

fun_fact.title: Scientists are now seriously debating whether bees — and chatbots — might be a little bit conscious.
fun_fact.body: A wave of 2026 research argues that consciousness can't be judged by behavior alone: a chatbot can discuss philosophy without feeling anything, and a bee searching for nectar might feel something without being able to say so. The honest takeaway isn't that your AI assistant has an inner life — it's that we still lack a reliable test for inner life in anything, which makes 'is it conscious?' a much harder question than the confident headlines suggest. Sweet dreams. 🐝
